text: In the year 2000, three men from a struggling little company flew to Dallas for the most important meeting of their lives.
Their business mailed DVDs to people's houses, and it was losing a lot of money. They'd come to ask the biggest name in home video to buy them. For fifty million dollars.
One of the men in that room later wrote that Blockbuster's chief executive was fighting to keep a straight face. He was trying not to laugh.
The little company was called Netflix.
Everybody knows that story. Blockbuster laughed, Netflix won, the end. But that's not what happened.
A few years later, Blockbuster figured it out. It built its own Netflix, and it was winning. And then it did something much dumber than laughing.

text: I'm Sam. This is Last Receipt. Tonight, the rise and fall of Blockbuster, and the boardroom fight that really killed it.

text: If you're over thirty-five, you can probably still smell it. Carpet, popcorn and plastic. Friday night, and the whole neighborhood is in there, walking the walls, looking for a movie that isn't already gone.

Blockbuster opened in Dallas in 1985, with thousands of titles and a computer that tracked every single one. Then Wayne Huizenga took over. He'd built a garbage-hauling company into the giant Waste Management. He didn't know movies. He knew how to open the same thing a thousand times, and for a while, Blockbuster opened about a store a day.
In 1994, Viacom paid more than eight billion dollars for it.
And underneath all of it was the thing everybody hated.
Late fees. In the year 2000, Blockbuster collected roughly eight hundred million dollars in late fees. About sixteen cents of every dollar it made.

text: Think about that. One of this company's biggest products was its customers' mistakes.

Netflix launched in 1998 with a flat monthly price, no due dates and no late fees. By 2000, it was on track to lose more than fifty million dollars that year, and the dot-com bubble had just burst.

headline: The pitch: fifty million dollars
sub: You run the stores. We run your online business.

text: So Reed Hastings, Marc Randolph and their finance chief, Barry McCarthy, went to Dallas with a pitch. You run the stores, we'll run your online business. Buy us for fifty million.
It's easy to laugh at Blockbuster here. But put yourself in that chair.
You're running a company with about five billion dollars in sales. Thousands of stores. And these guys, losing money mailing discs in envelopes, want fifty million.
camText: And these guys, losing money mailing discs in envelopes, want fifty million.

text: In the year 2000, hardly anybody even owned a DVD player. Saying no wasn't crazy. Saying no was the sensible thing to do.
camText: Saying no wasn't crazy. Saying no was the sensible thing to do.

headline: Blockbuster signs a twenty-year deal to send movies over the internet

text: And Blockbuster wasn't ignoring the future. That same year, it signed a twenty-year deal to deliver movies over the internet, straight to your TV. The partner was Enron.
That deal fell apart within months. So Blockbuster went back to what it knew. Stores.

Then three things happened, and none of them looked like an emergency. DVDs got cheap enough to buy instead of rent. Netflix went public in 2002 and passed a million subscribers in 2003. And a red vending machine called Redbox started renting movies outside supermarkets for a dollar a night.

Right then, in 2004, Viacom spun Blockbuster off. On the way out, Blockbuster borrowed to pay its shareholders a huge one-time dividend. It walked into the hardest fight of its life carrying roughly a billion dollars in debt.
Here's the thing about debt. When business is good, nobody notices it. When business turns, it's the only thing anyone notices.

headline: John Antioco, Blockbuster CEO
sub: Before that: Taco Bell and Circle K

text: The man running Blockbuster was John Antioco, the executive from that meeting. He'd turned around Taco Bell and Circle K, and he was not a fool. And he made two decisions that could have saved the company.

headline: Blockbuster Online
sub: DVDs by mail, flat monthly price

text: In 2004, Blockbuster launched Blockbuster Online. DVDs by mail, flat monthly price. Netflix in a blue envelope, four years late.
Then, on January first, 2005, it ended late fees. Hundreds of millions of dollars a year, given up on purpose. The whole plan was expected to cost around four hundred million dollars.
Now watch this. For about a year, it wasn't working. And then somebody at Blockbuster had the best idea in the history of the company.

headline: Blockbuster Total Access
sub: Rent by mail. Swap the envelope in any store.

text: It was called Total Access. Rent by mail, and instead of mailing the movie back, walk into any store, hand over the envelope and walk out with a new one. Free. Right then. Netflix's weakness was the wait. Blockbuster had thousands of stores full of movies. Netflix didn't have a single one.
Blockbuster Online passed two million subscribers. And in the spring of 2007, Netflix did something it had almost never done. It lost subscribers.
Seven years after the laugh, the company that was losing was Netflix.
What Blockbuster didn't have was a board that agreed with its own chief executive.

headline: Carl Icahn wins seats on the Blockbuster board

text: In 2005, the investor Carl Icahn had bought a big stake in Blockbuster and won seats on its board. From where Icahn sat, Antioco's plan looked like a bonfire. Ending late fees cost a fortune. Total Access lost money on every swap. The online service was burning cash to grow. And to be fair, the board wasn't wrong about the math.
This is the hard part of every one of these stories. The thing that saves you in five years is usually the thing that hurts you this quarter.
camText: This is the hard part of every one of these stories.

text: It finally snapped over Antioco's bonus. The board cut it, he fought it, and in 2007, in the middle of the one strategy that was working, he agreed to leave.
His replacement, Jim Keyes, had run 7-Eleven. He raised prices on Total Access, pulled back on the online fight, and put the focus back on the stores.

Netflix started growing again almost immediately. And that January, it had quietly launched a little feature that let you watch a movie instantly on your computer. Hardly anyone noticed. It was called streaming.

In September 2010, Blockbuster filed for bankruptcy. Dish bought what was left for around three hundred and twenty million dollars. This was a company that had sold for more than eight billion. By 2014, the last company-owned stores in America were gone.

Except one. A franchise store in Bend, Oregon, still rents movies, and people fly in from around the world to stand in its aisles. And Netflix, the company Blockbuster could have had for fifty million dollars, went on to be worth well over a hundred billion.
So what killed Blockbuster? Everybody says Netflix. Everybody says the laugh in that meeting.

text: I don't buy it. Saying no in 2000 was a reasonable mistake. The real mistake came in 2007, when it was finally winning, and decided winning cost too much.

text: It had the answer. And it fired the plan to protect the profits of a business that was already dying.
Companies don't usually die because they can't see the future. They die because the future is expensive, and the past is still paying the bills.
